strengths: The paper addresses a relevant NLP problem: evaluating document coherence across different texts and lengths. SPM offers an interpretable extension of Brownian-bridge scoring through temporal and cross-dimensional covariance, with explicit likelihood and covariance-estimation derivations.

The reported metric improvements are substantial in the evaluated synthetic settings. With the contrastive encoder, SPM achieves 94.72–95.67% global-shuffle accuracy and 77.89–90.32% mixed-shuffle accuracy on WikiSection, consistently outperforming BBScore. These results support further investigation of the metric independently of the proposed encoder.

Experiments cover several perturbation scales, local and global discrimination, two transfer corpora, and HC3. The paper supplies mathematical derivations and some training details, and acknowledges weaker performance on local perturbations.
weaknesses: The central encoder objective has an unresolved collapse problem (Section 2.2.2). A constant encoder makes all bridge residuals zero. More generally, scaling representations by a and their estimated covariance by a² preserves the quadratic term while driving the log-determinant contribution toward negative infinity as a approaches zero. The proposed variance-scaled shrinkage does not remove this degeneracy. Appendix B's modification to fixed identity regularization can bound the objective, but still does not prevent constant representations. Thus, minimizing this loss does not establish information preservation or learning of nondegenerate Brownian dynamics; an explicit remedy and training diagnostics are needed.

The encoder's claimed superiority is stronger than the evidence. In Table 4, SP underperforms CL in every in-domain condition; mixed-shuffle accuracy at block size 10 drops from 77.89% to 53.97%. Table 5 shows some useful transfer gains, but also regressions and approximately chance-level WSJ results for larger blocks. Covariance visualizations do not establish that dimensional utilization causes generalization improvements, and the absence of repeated runs or uncertainty estimates limits interpretation of smaller gains.

The theoretical claims exceed what is proved. Propositions 1–2 derive a Gaussian likelihood and its covariance estimator, rather than establishing superiority over competing metrics. Even with the true covariance, SPM follows χ²_k/k, where k=(T−1)d: its expectation is length-independent, but its variance is 2/k. Consequently, normalization does not establish a length-independent score distribution or calibrated comparability on real text. Controlled ablations separating temporal covariance, structural covariance, and normalization are also missing.

The coherence evidence primarily establishes sensitivity to synthetic ordering corruption. There is no validation against human judgments of naturally occurring coherence, and the mixed-shuffle test assumes that an original article should outrank shuffled versions of unrelated articles. Furthermore, Table 2 omits Unified Coherence despite the accompanying claim of outperforming state-of-the-art methods. Pairwise training alone does not demonstrate that a baseline cannot compare documents of different lengths.

The human–AI experiment is insufficiently specified and supports a narrower conclusion than claimed. It is unclear whether accuracy measures paired ranking or thresholded classification of individual texts, and HC3 sample counts and pairing details are missing. The headline comparison uses DetectGPT with one perturbation; Table 8 reports 84.89% and 83.13% with ten perturbations, substantially above SPM's 70.67% and 69.71%. This suggests a possible accuracy–computation tradeoff, but inference counts without specified model configurations and measured runtimes do not establish the claimed latency advantage.

Reproducibility remains incomplete: the covariance-fitting protocol for out-of-domain evaluation, validation data used to select epsilon, long-document preprocessing, and CL/SPM+CLS training configurations are insufficiently documented in the supplied manuscript. Appendix B also changes the regularization described in the method. The promising metric results make next-cycle resubmission worthwhile, but the encoder's soundness problem and these evaluation gaps currently prevent a clear Findings recommendation.
